Matrix Multiplication. A fundamental algebraic operation that combines two matrices to produce a third matrix, representing the composition of linear transformations. The computational efficiency of multiplying matrices is a major area of study in computer science because it is a core bottleneck in graphics, physics simulations, and machine learning.

The standard, naive algorithm for multiplying two n by n matrices requires O of n cubed arithmetic operations, directly performing the dot products of rows and columns. In 1969, Strassen's algorithm was the first to show that matrix multiplication could be done faster than O of n cubed. It uses a divide-and-conquer strategy that reduces the number of sub-multiplications from eight to seven, yielding a runtime of O of n to the power of log base two of seven, which is approximately O of n to the power of 2.81.

The asymptotic complexity limit of matrix multiplication is denoted by the Greek letter omega, representing the lower bound of exponents such that two n by n matrices can be multiplied in O of n to omega operations. The Coppersmith-Winograd algorithm established a theoretical bound of O of n to the power of 2.376 in 1987, and modern refinements have lowered this bound to approximately O of n to the power of 2.371.

Despite their theoretical speed, algorithms with exponents below Strassen's are rarely used in practice because they have extremely large hidden constant factors—referred to as galactic algorithms. Matrix multiplication is a polynomial-time operation located securely in the class P. The exact lower bound for matrix multiplication remains an open question, whereas comparison-based sorting has a known lower bound of O of n log n. The all-pairs shortest path problem can be solved by translating it into min-plus matrix multiplication, and the matrix chain multiplication problem, which finds the most efficient order to multiply a sequence of matrices, is solved using dynamic programming similar to the knapsack problem.
